Stage 3 · Grammar

Six ways to tell someone what to do

They all mean roughly the same thing. They do not all sound the same.

Read these five sentences. They all come from the recordings later in this lesson.
  • You should take it easy.
  • You mustn’t lift anything heavy.
  • You could try this cream, which should help.
  • It’s a good idea to keep your windows closed at night.
  • I don’t think you should feel bad.
What form of the verb comes after should, could and ought to?
The six forms, from strongest to softest
FormExampleHow it lands
You must / mustn’t + baseYou mustn’t lift anything heavy.an order — doctor, boss, sign
You should / shouldn’t + baseYou should take it easy.the normal advice form
You ought to + baseYou ought to see a doctor.same as should, a little more formal
You could + baseYou could try this cream.one option among several
Why don’t you + base?Why don’t you call them?friendly, spoken, a suggestion
It’s a good idea to + baseIt’s a good idea to keep the windows closed.general advice, not personal
fixed phrase If I were you, I’d + baseIf I were you, I’d stick to one page.learn it whole — do not change the verbs
Put the four forms in order, from the strongest to the softest.

FORM. should / shouldn’t / could / must + base form, no to. Only ought to keeps its to.

QUESTIONS. Should I…? What should I do? Do you think I should…?

SOFTENING. I don’t think you should… is much gentler than You shouldn’t….

Not “You should to go”, not “You should going”, not “I advice you” (the verb is advise).

If I were you is a fixed opener at this level. The grammar behind it comes in Unit 11.

FORM. should, shouldn’t, could and must are followed by the base form with no to: You should rest. The one exception is ought to, which carries its own to: You ought to rest. Neither form changes for he / she / it — never he shoulds.

ASKING FOR ADVICE. What should I do? · Should I call them? · Do you think I should apply? · Have you got any advice about…? Note the word order: should comes before the subject in a question.

CHOOSING THE STRENGTH. must is an order and sounds hard from a friend. should is the everyday advice form. could offers one option and leaves the decision with the other person. Why don’t you…? is warm and spoken. Learners at this level reach for must far too often; should is almost always the right choice.

SOFTENING A NEGATIVE. You shouldn’t worry is direct. I don’t think you should worry is kinder and just as clear — and it is what the doctor says in the recording.

Four mistakes to watch: “You should to rest” · “He shoulds rest” · “I advice you to rest” (advice is the noun, advise is the verb) · “If I was you” (the fixed phrase keeps were).

LOOKING AHEAD. If I were you, I’d… is a second conditional. At this level, learn it as one whole phrase and change only the part after I’d. Unit 11 takes it apart.

Five sentences from Navigate B1 Audio 9.8. Press Listen to hear each one.

Full grammar reference — Giving advice

Form

NeutralYou should take it easy. · You shouldn’t work so late.
A little strongerYou ought to tell her. · You need to rest.
A suggestionWhy don’t you take a few days off? · How about talking to her?
Putting yourself thereIf I were you, I’d talk to him.
Asking for adviceWhat should I do? · What would you do?

When and why we use it

  • Should is followed by the plain verb; Why don’t you is followed by the plain verb; How about is followed by -ing.
  • If I were you keeps were for every person — it is a fixed phrase.
  • Give a reason with the advice; advice without a reason sounds like an order.
  • In a formal letter, advice becomes a suggestion: It might be worth…

Signal words

if I were you · I’d · perhaps · maybe · it might be worth

Watch out — the mistakes learners really make

  • You should to rest. → You should rest.No to after should.
  • Why don’t you to call her? → Why don’t you call her?Plain verb.
  • How about to meet? → How about meeting?How about + -ing.
  • If I was you, I’d wait. → If I were you, I’d wait.Fixed phrase with were.

Don’t confuse it with

You should = advice. You have to = a rule. You must = strong necessity. Advice is the softest of the three.

Stage 5 · The model

The covering letter

Read it the way a writer reads it: not for the news, but for the shape and the phrases.

Read the whole letter once. Do not answer anything yet.

A covering letter

Aisha Karimova
aisha.karimova@mail.com
+7 701 000 00 00
14 March

Dear Ms Whitfield,

1  I am writing to apply for the position of Junior Outdoor Instructor, which I saw advertised on your website on 10 March.

2  I am currently finishing a degree in Sport Science and I will graduate in June. During my studies I have worked for two summers at a children’s adventure camp, where I was responsible for groups of twelve and for their safety in all weather. I also run a small cycling club in my city.

3  I am applying for this position because your philosophy of natural, outdoor movement is exactly the way I want to work. I am fit, calm with beginners, and used to gentle progress rather than fast results.

4  I attach my CV and two references. I am available for an interview at any time, and I can start as soon as the university year finishes.

5  Thank you for considering my application. I look forward to hearing from you.

Yours sincerely,
Aisha Karimova

Note. Written for this course as a writing model. Aisha Karimova, Ms Whitfield and the company are invented; the layout follows standard British covering-letter order.

Useful language — the covering letter

Open: I am writing to apply for the position of… · which I saw advertised on…
You: I am currently… · During my studies I have worked… · I was responsible for…
Why them: I am applying because… · Your philosophy of… is exactly…
Practical: I attach… · I am available for an interview… · I can start as soon as…
Close: Thank you for considering my application. · I look forward to hearing from you. · Yours sincerely / Yours faithfully

Now you

First the advice out loud, then the letter on the page.

Useful language — asking for and giving advice

Asking: Can I ask your advice about…? · What should I do? · Do you think I should…? · Have you got any advice about…?
Giving: You should… · You ought to… · You could… · Why don’t you…? · It’s a good idea to… · If I were you, I’d… · I don’t think you should…
Reacting: That’s a good idea. · I hadn’t thought of that. · I’m not sure that would work for me.

1 · Work in pairs. Student A has the problem, Student B gives advice. Then swap.
Student A — your problem

You have applied for eleven jobs and had no answer at all. You send the same letter every time. You are starting to feel depressed about it. Your graduation was in June. Ask for advice — and do not accept the first thing you hear.

Student B — you give advice

You have hired people before. You think the letter matters more than the CV, that one page is enough, and that nobody should apply for a job they do not want. Give at least four pieces of advice, in four different forms.

Six to eight exchanges. Then swap cards: B has a new problem — a back that hurts after every long drive.
